A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ONEBench research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison. Material relocated or renumbered in v2 can be matched to v1.

before.justification: v1 reports original aggregation comparisons, missing-data experiments, retrieval evaluations with human annotations, and capability-specific model rankings.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, synthetic simulations, separability experiments, and quantitative analyses of capability-specific rankings.

M1.justification: Both versions use sample pooling, conversion to ordinal rankings, structured and embedding-based retrieval, and Plackett-Luce aggregation with partial rank breaking. Expanded evaluation and relocated mathematical descriptions do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: The real benchmark inventory and the 40 LLM/50 LMM concept coverage are retained, including their appendix listings. Appendix D in v2 adds a controlled synthetic ranking environment with numerical, binary and ordinal measurements, providing limited additional coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates aggregation against Elo and LMArena. v2 retains these and adds Borda Count and the Dowdall System across the four real benchmarks in Table 2. Section 4.3 also introduces random retrieval as a comparator for capability-based retrieval, substantially broadening the comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include Gumbel simulations with 100 systems and 1,000 measurements, dispersion and missingness sweeps, equal-half partition tests, retrieval comparisons at 100/1,000/10,000 samples, and top-5/top-10 ranking comparisons. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original benchmark setup and retrieval thresholds remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's sample-removal and sparsity experiments, v2 adds synthetic sensitivity tests, checks whether consistent subset rankings survive aggregation, controls capability queries against random subsets, and quantifies differences between global and capability-specific top rankings. These additions in Section 4.3 and Appendices D, E and F.2 address substantial new diagnostic questions.

E5.justification: The original three-run mean/variance reporting is retained. v2 adds five random-retrieval repetitions, five partition repetitions with explicit mean/standard-deviation reporting, and Wilcoxon signed-rank statistics and p-values in Table 11. No increase in the original experiments' run count is stated.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear in Tables 2, 4, 7–9 and 11. For example, Table 2 reports LMMs-Eval correlations of 0.64 for ONEBench, 0.08 for Borda and 0.18 for Dowdall; Table 9 reports 100% separability consistency for both Plackett-Luce and LMArena. Per-concept AP values are retained, while neuroscience and Gothic-architecture qualitative ranking examples are omitted.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's active-aggregation/PAC property discussion and adds definitions and stated violations of pairwise majority consistency and separability in Section 7. The principal likelihood, identifiability and sample-complexity statements remain, without new proofs. The rewritten model-set definition also introduces an apparent intersection-for-union error.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain open-ended sample-level benchmarking, aggregation of heterogeneous and incomplete measurements, personalized capability queries, and LLM/LMM instantiations. Both versions retain the headline robustness and up-to-20-fold evaluation-cost claims. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 adds an external-validity and benchmark-longevity rationale for rankings, acknowledges that mean-score ground truth is suboptimal, and interprets the new baseline and query-control results. Section 7 introduces substantive limitations concerning reproducibility, modeling assumptions, and violated aggregation axioms. The original future directions are retained in Appendix H.

D1.justification: v2 documents synthetic-data generation and explains reproducibility through specifying sample identifiers. Its front matter replaces the direct dataset link with a project-page link while retaining the code link. Two model identifiers in Appendix B.1 are shortened, reducing checkpoint specificity; most existing dataset and retrieval details remain available.

R1.justification: Most related work is retained in Appendix G. v2 adds positioning around ranking stability and benchmark longevity through Recht et al., Salaudeen and Hardt, and Hardt and Recht, plus Noothigattu et al. on aggregation axioms. Several citations, including those supporting the removed active-aggregation discussion, are dropped without fundamentally changing the research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the main text are substantially condensed and rewritten. Detailed ranking definitions, dataset descriptions, extended related work and future directions move into appendices. The main contents list and introductory verse disappear, and dedicated Limitations and Broad Impacts sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, retained summary tables are transposed, and six result tables are added. Dataset displays move to Appendix A. v1 Figure 5 becomes v2 Figure 4 with two concept rows removed, while the additional qualitative Figure 6 is retained.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked known-truth simulations and random-subset controls for its capability-specific rankings. v2 adds both, expands aggregation baselines, and explicitly discusses violated axioms and other limitations. Together these substantially strengthen validation of the aggregation and personalization claims. Minor notation and documentation regressions, and fewer illustrative examples, do not outweigh the gains in evidence and qualification.
